cloze.instruction: 从词库中选择合适的词填入空白，每词使用一次，保留原文词形。大小写不影响判分。

parts.text: Typically, when people hear about nitrates, it involves runoff from farm fields, sewage systems and cities that can fuel

algae blooms and raise the risk of a serious illness in infants known as “blue baby syndrome.”

But a river can also run through a sparsely populated landscape with little farming and still contain surprisingly high levels of this form of

that can harm aquatic life, drinking water and human health.

In a new study, my colleague and I found a reason why that happens: Dry climate conditions are associated with high river nitrate

, even in places with little farming or urban development.

We found nitrate hot spots in some unexpected places, including the Rocky Mountains of the western United States and northern Africa’s Sahara Desert. Where water is

, we found that nitrates – which can naturally leach into surface water and groundwater from the soil as microbes break down organic material – were able to accumulate and become concentrated rather than being diluted or

away.

That raises health concerns for regions where nitrates in rivers and well water might not be given much thought. It also raises questions about how nitrate-related health risks will increase as global temperatures rise.

To see how

this pattern is, we combined global measurements from more than 7,000 monitoring sites and additionally extracted information about climate, soils, land use and other landscape features. We then trained machine learning models to

long-term average nitrate concentrations across nearly 2.9 million river segments worldwide.

The resulting map suggests that nitrates deserve attention well beyond the urban and

regions where they are usually monitored.

Why it matters

High nitrate exposure in water and food is particularly dangerous for infants because it can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen. Blue baby syndrome, or methemoglobinemia, can result in serious illnesses and be caused by nitrate

.

The U.S. drinking water standard of 10 milligrams of nitrate-nitrogen per liter was established primarily to guard against this acute risk.

We estimate that about 37,000 people worldwide live in areas where rivers
the 10 mg/L drinking water standard, predominantly in the U.S. Corn Belt.
